title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
text:
When the bus stopped running to Kheda village during the rains, the small library in the panchayat hall became the busiest room for miles. It had only two shelves, a mat and a window that let in a square of grey light, but every afternoon children came in with wet feet and left with their heads full of other places.

The library was looked after by Meena, a girl of fourteen who had been given the key because, as the sarpanch said, she was the only person who always returned it. Meena did not simply hand out books. She noticed who lingered near the picture books and who pretended not to care. She would leave a book about trains beside a boy who loved engines, or read the first page of a mystery aloud and then stop, so that the listeners had to finish it themselves.

Some elders grumbled that reading stories was a waste of time when there was work to be done. Meena never argued. Instead, she asked the children to write down the stories their grandparents told, and soon the shelves held a new kind of book: thin notebooks full of village songs, old floods and remedies for coughs. The grumbling became quieter. It is hard to call reading useless when your own words are on the shelf.

title: Read the poem and answer the questions that follow.
text:
The clouds came marching over the hill,
With drums of thunder, loud and shrill;
The dusty field held up its face,
And waited for the rain's embrace.

The first drops fell like scattered seeds,
On thirsty roots and tired weeds;
The frogs began their evening choir,
The farmer smiled beside his fire.

O patient earth, you never ask,
Yet bear each season's heavy task;
You wait through heat without a sound,
Then bloom the moment rain is found.

title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
text:
Long before taps and pipelines, people in the dry western parts of India found clever ways to save every drop of rain. One of the most beautiful was the stepwell, a deep well reached by long flights of stone steps. As the water level rose in the monsoon and fell in summer, people simply walked down as many steps as they needed to reach it.

Stepwells were more than places to collect water. Because they went deep into the ground, the air at the bottom stayed cool even in the hottest months, and travellers rested there in the shade. Many were decorated with carved pillars and arches, which shows how much the community valued them.

When piped water arrived, many stepwells were neglected. Rubbish collected in them and some were filled in completely. In recent years, however, several towns have cleaned and repaired their old stepwells. Engineers have found that these structures still help to recharge groundwater, the water stored beneath the soil. In a time of falling water tables, an old idea is proving to be surprisingly modern.

title: Read the poem and answer the questions that follow.
text:
Before the sun has rubbed its eyes,
The market starts to wake and rise;
The sabziwala sets his rows
Of ladyfinger, beans and tomatoes.

The tea is boiling, sweet and strong,
The kettle hums a whistling song;
A cart rolls by with squeaking wheels,
And sells hot rotis, simple meals.

By noon the busy crowd is gone,
The empty baskets, one by one,
Are stacked away beneath the shade,
Till morning when the stalls are made.

title: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
text:
When the children of Class 4 at a small school in Nashik asked their teacher why the school had no garden, she gave them a surprising answer: 'Because nobody has made one yet.' The next week, a corner of the playground that had been full of broken bricks was cleared by thirty pairs of small hands.

The children soon discovered that gardening was full of questions. Why did the spinach grow well near the wall but wilt in the open? Why did ants march up the stems of the brinjal plants? They measured, they argued, and they kept a diary with drawings of every plant. One boy, who rarely spoke in class, became the expert on earthworms and was always asked to explain why they were good for the soil.

By the end of the year, the garden had given the school three baskets of vegetables for the midday meal. But the teacher said the real harvest was something else. The children had learned to wonder, to test their guesses and to listen to one another.
